official.deadline_central_display: Early Action November 30; Regular Action February 15; Transfer February 15 (identical for domestic and international students)
official.deadline_note: MIT publishes these as annual cycle dates without a calendar year. Continuing students reapply by February 15 and receive offers in late May or early June.
official.application_cycle: Annual cycle aligned to MIT's admission rounds (Early Action, Regular Action, Transfer)
official.status_note: Aid applications follow the published admission-cycle deadlines on MIT Student Financial Services.
official.tuition_coverage_note: Published wording: "students from families with an annual income under $200,000 ... typically attend MIT tuition-free" and MIT is "committed to meeting 100% of demonstrated financial need with our aid" for all undergraduates, domestic and international.
benefits: Need-blind, full-need admissions for all undergraduates, domestic and international - MIT commits to meeting 100% of demonstrated financial need
MIT Scholarship, a grant that does not need to be repaid; 58% of full-time undergraduates received one in 2025-2026
Students from families with annual income under $200,000 typically attend tuition-free; for families with income below $100,000 parents can expect to pay nothing toward the full cost of attendance
First Year Grant of $2,000 for highest-need first-year students, split equally between fall and spring
Health Insurance Grant covering the MIT Student Health Insurance Plan for highest-need undergraduates who lack adequate coverage
eligibility: Classified as international for financial aid purposes - not eligible for federal student financial aid as determined by the FAFSA
Applies for undergraduate admission to MIT
Awarding is based solely on demonstrated financial need; about 58% of MIT undergraduates receive an MIT Scholarship
requirements: Submit the CSS Profile designating MIT with CSS Code 3514 and answer all MIT supplemental questions
Submit parents' tax returns or income documentation to the College Board's Institutional Documentation Service (IDOC) - documents sent directly to MIT cannot be accepted
Provide the tax return from a parent's home country with a translation to English if applicable (self-translation acceptable)
documents: CSS Profile (College Board) designating MIT, CSS Code 3514
Parents' income tax returns or wage statements from two years ago
Records of untaxed income, current bank account balances and records of investments
English translations of non-U.S. tax documents; both parents' income documentation if parents are separated or divorced
selection_criteria: Aid is awarded on the basis of financial need alone - there is no merit component
Late applications carry no penalty but are decided later; applications must be received before the end of the academic year (mid-May for most students, mid-December for fall-only attendees)
coverage: Tuition and fees up to 100% of MIT's calculated demonstrated need through the MIT Scholarship
Housing, dining, fees and allowances for books and personal expenses within the full cost of attendance
First Year Grant of $2,000 (highest-need first-year students) and Health Insurance Grant (highest-need students lacking coverage)
application_method: Submit the CSS Profile online through the College Board with MIT code 3514
Submit parental tax returns or income documentation to College Board IDOC
Track documents and view the offer through the MIT Application Portal ("Track Financial Aid Documents") and the MIT Online Financial Aid System
official.application_route: CSS Profile plus IDOC documentation submitted by the admission-round deadline (Early Action November 30; Regular Action or Transfer February 15).
official.citizenship_residency: No citizenship or residency restriction - international students follow the same process as domestic applicants
official.international_eligibility: Yes - international students are considered for aid using the same process as all applicants, and MIT commits to meeting 100% of demonstrated need for them
official.duration: Aid is awarded for each academic year of the undergraduate degree and reviewed annually; continuing students reapply by February 15
official.description: MIT is need-blind and full-need for all undergraduate students, domestic and international: it is committed to meeting 100% of demonstrated financial need, and 58% of full-time undergraduates received an MIT Scholarship in 2025-2026.

verification.notes: The international application process, CSS code 3514, IDOC routing, admission-round deadlines and the need-met commitment were read directly from sfs.mit.edu pages on 2026-10-10. No fixed award amount is published; aid is calculated per family, with published medians (e.g. $85,236 median MIT Scholarship for the $0-$100,000 income band) recorded as statistics in benefits. Students remain expected to contribute through summer savings and term-time work, so fully_funded is not asserted.

applicant_utility.summary: MIT runs need-blind, full-need admissions for international undergraduates: if you are admitted with need, MIT commits to covering all of it through the same CSS Profile process domestic students use. The aid deadlines match the admission rounds - November 30 for Early Action, February 15 for Regular Action and Transfer - and continuing students reapply every February 15. In 2025-26, 58% of undergraduates held an MIT Scholarship and the median net price for recipients was $11,432, but every student is still expected to contribute through summer savings and term-time work.
applicant_utility.best_fit: Admitted international undergraduates whose families cannot fund MIT's cost of attendance and can document income and assets in detail.
application_readiness_checklist: Submit the CSS Profile with MIT code 3514 and answer every MIT supplemental question
Send parents' income documents to College Board IDOC, not to MIT - allow up to two weeks for delivery plus 10 business days for processing
Pull tax documents from two years ago (prior-prior year), not the most recent filing
Translate foreign tax documents yourself if needed - professional translation is not required
Check "Documents & Messages" in the MIT Online Financial Aid System rather than emailing the office
common_rejection_risks: Missing the aid deadline for your admission round and losing first-round consideration
Sending documents directly to MIT - they are refused; everything routes through IDOC
Assuming aid continues automatically - continuing students must reapply by February 15
Leaving the application incomplete past mid-May, which forfeits aid for that academic year
Overlooking that separated or divorced parents each need their own CSS Profile and income documentation
applicant_utility.estimated_uncovered_costs: Students are expected to contribute from summer savings and term-time work; MIT calculates offers so that loans should not be needed, but that expected student contribution remains yours to fund.
document_audit: Tax documents are prior-prior year - two years back, not last year's filing
Foreign parents' returns need an English translation attached
Untaxed income, current bank balances and investment records are all requested - gaps delay review
Both parents' income documentation is required when parents are separated or divorced
alerts: Late applications carry no penalty but decisions come later - submit by mid-May at the latest
Fall-only attendees must submit their aid application by mid-December
Offers arrive mid-January for Early Action and mid-March for Regular Action
The Health Insurance Grant and the $2,000 First Year Grant go only to the highest-need students
applicant_utility.submission_workflow: CSS Profile plus IDOC documents by the round deadline, tracked through the MIT Application Portal; the offer arrives by email from sfs@mit.edu.
